h1: The 8 Best Grapefruit Knives of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 grapefruit knives scored on blade curve, serration, handle material, length and cleanup, all under $30.
summary: The Norpro Twin Blades with a rosewood handle is the grapefruit knife to buy if you want the classic double-ended design done properly. The Norpro Nonstick Squirtless adds a release coating and a longer 8.75 inch body, the Reluen is the best dishwasher-safe pick, and the Fox Run is the lightest, at 1.41 ounces. Every knife in this ranking sits under $30, so the real decision is handle material and how much cleanup you will tolerate.
intro: Most people blame the fruit when a grapefruit half turns into a juice puddle. The knife is usually the culprit. A grapefruit knife has one job, which is to cut the pulp free of the rind and then free of each membrane wall, and a blade with the wrong curve or dull serrations tears sections instead of lifting them out whole.

This ranking covers eight knives, all in the under $30 bracket, and sorts them by blade geometry first and handle second. We reviewed the listed lengths, blade styles, handle materials and care instructions, and we ranked each one against the others rather than against an imaginary ideal. Where a listing does not say something, such as blade steel grade, we leave it out instead of guessing.

products.name: Norpro Twin Blades Grapefruit Knife, 8 inch
products.verdict: The classic double-ended design with a contoured rosewood grip, and the most balanced knife here.
products.description:
The Norpro Twin Blades is an 8 inch knife with a serrated stainless blade at each end of a contoured rosewood handle. One end has curved twin edges built to run between pulp and membrane, and the other has a reverse serrated edge for separating the fruit from the rind. That double-ended layout is the original grapefruit knife formula, and this is the cleanest execution of it in the group.

It ranks first because the handle sits in the middle and the weight stays centered, so you can flip ends without re-gripping. The nonstick Norpro below it releases pulp a little easier, but it asks for more care around the coating, and the wood here feels more controlled when the fruit is wet. The Reluen offers dishwasher cleanup that this knife cannot match, which is the real tradeoff.

Buy it if you eat grapefruit several mornings a week and want a knife that feels like a proper tool. Skip it if you load everything into the dishwasher, because a natural rosewood handle wants a quick hand wash and a dry towel after each use.
products.idealFor: Regular grapefruit eaters who want one knife that handles both the rind cut and the section cut.
products.skipIf: You want a dishwasher-safe knife with zero care routine.

products.name: Norpro Nonstick Squirtless Grapefruit Knife, 8.75 inch
products.verdict: A nonstick-coated, dishwasher-safe knife with an oversized handle that suits larger hands.
products.description:
At 8.75 inches, this is the longest knife in the ranking, with nonstick-coated stainless blades on a yellow and red oversized handle. The curved twin blades work the membrane side while a separate serrated edge handles the rind. Norpro lists it as dishwasher safe and usable in either hand.

The coating is what separates it from the rosewood Norpro above. Pulp slides off the blade instead of clinging to the serrations, which cuts down on the stop-and-wipe rhythm during a full breakfast prep. It lands second because plastic does not have the dense feel of wood, and a coating will always wear faster than bare steel with enough scrubbing.

This is the pick for people with larger or arthritic hands who want a fatter grip, and for households that put everything through the dishwasher. The caveat is length. At 8.75 inches it is a little long for small drawers, and anyone with small hands may find the handle bulkier than they want.
cons: Longest knife, awkward in tight drawers
products.idealFor: Anyone who wants an easy-grip, easy-clean knife and prefers a chunkier handle.
products.skipIf: You have small hands or like the weight and feel of a wood handle.

products.name: Reluen Curved Serrated Grapefruit Knife
products.verdict: A curved dual-serrated stainless blade that also handles oranges and lemons, and goes straight in the dishwasher.
products.description:
The Reluen uses a curved, double-serrated stainless steel blade on a non-slip handle, and its listing places it for grapefruit, oranges and lemons alike. It measures about 8.66 inches overall and is listed as dishwasher safe, with a rust-resistant finish promised for repeated cycles.

It sits third because it is a single-blade design. The two Norpro knives above give you a separate rind-cutting end, so they do more of the job without switching tools. Where the Reluen pulls ahead of the cheaper models below is fit: the handle is shaped to stay grippy when your hands are wet, which is the exact condition of a grapefruit session.

It suits cooks who also segment oranges and lemons for salads, and anyone who values a handle that does not need hand washing. The honest limit is that you will need a paring knife or spoon to loosen the fruit from the rind first, because the blade is built for the membrane cut rather than both steps.
products.idealFor: Cooks who segment all kinds of citrus and want easy dishwasher cleanup.
products.skipIf: You want a second blade at the other end for the rind cut.

products.name: Fox Run 6601 Grapefruit Knife
products.verdict: A 1.41 ounce dual-ended knife that stays out of your way, at the cost of some heft.
products.description:
The Fox Run 6601 is a dual-ended knife at 7.75 inches long and 1.41 ounces, with a curved blade on one end and a finely serrated edge on the other. The middle grip is smooth, which gives you a position to hold without the blade ends sliding forward.

It ranks fourth because it is lighter and more compact than the Norpro pair, and light knives respond quickly but give you less cutting momentum through a thick rind. For a thin-skinned fruit like a pink grapefruit that is fine. For a tough one you will feel the Norpro knives pushing through with less effort.

This knife works for kitchens with short drawer space or for anyone who prefers a light touch. Buy it if you cut one or two grapefruit a week. The caveat is that the listing is vague about the exact handle material and finish, so treat it as a hand-wash-only piece to be safe.
cons: Less cutting momentum on thick rind
products.idealFor: Light users and small kitchens that want a dual-ended knife without bulk.
products.skipIf: You regularly cut dense, thick-skinned grapefruit.

products.name: Chef Craft Select Grapefruit Knife with Wood Handle
products.verdict: A straightforward 7.5 inch knife with a 3.75 inch curved, double-serrated blade and a wood grip.
products.description:
The Chef Craft Select is a plain, honest tool: a 3.75 inch curved stainless blade serrated on both edges, attached to a wood handle for a total length of 7.5 inches. The curve is meant to sweep around each membrane, and the stainless blade is listed as rust-free through repeated use.

It lands fifth because it does one thing and nothing else. There is no second blade end, no coating and no oversized grip, so it trails the Norpro models on features. The blade length is a genuine plus, though. A 3.75 inch blade reaches into the center of a large half without the handle brushing the rind, which the shorter-bladed knives lower in this list can struggle with.

It suits buyers who want a no-fuss wood handle at the lowest practical cost. The caveat is care: the maker states hand wash only, and a wood handle left soaking in the sink will crack or darken over a year of use.
products.idealFor: Basic citrus prep where you want a longer blade and a wood grip.
products.skipIf: You rely on the dishwasher for everything.

products.name: Better Houseware Grapefruit Knife with Nylon Handle
products.verdict: A no-maintenance nylon-handled knife with an angled tip that parts membrane from pulp.
products.description:
Better Houseware pairs a double-serrated stainless steel blade with a nylon handle, listed at about 8.25 inches overall and dishwasher safe. Its angled tip is designed to slip along the membrane wall and free each section, and the nylon grip does not absorb water the way untreated wood does.

It ranks sixth because nylon has less feel than wood or an oversized molded grip, and it offers nothing beyond the basic cut. The Chef Craft above has a longer 3.75 inch blade, and the Reluen offers a more contoured hold. This knife is the one to choose when durability and low care outweigh refinement.

It is a sensible spare for a second kitchen or a cabin. The caveat is grip comfort over a long session: after cutting four or five grapefruit for a brunch, the slimmer handle can feel less forgiving than the Norpro oversized grip.
cons: Slim grip tires on big batches
products.idealFor: A low-maintenance backup knife for a second kitchen.
products.skipIf: You prep a lot of fruit at once and want a bigger grip.

products.name: ModaSin Grapefruit Knife with Nonstick Plating
products.verdict: A thick-gauge, nonstick-plated knife that doubles as a kiwi and dessert tool.
products.description:
The ModaSin is a stainless knife with serrations on both sides of the blade, a thick-gauge handle and a nonstick plating. The listing positions it for kiwi, mango, apple and dessert use as well as citrus, and describes the saw-tooth edge as smooth enough to avoid scratching skin or mouth.

It ranks seventh because the multi-fruit promise is a stretch. A grapefruit knife works on grapefruit and oranges, but a blunt serrated edge is a poor choice for a ripe mango or an apple, and the listing says little about blade length or exact weight. The thick handle does help in wet hands, which gives it an edge over the plain nylon-handled knife below it.

Pick it for the flatware-style look, which pairs easily with other table pieces, or if you like serving grapefruit at the table. The caveat is that missing dimensions make it hard to judge fit, so confirm the listing before you commit.
products.idealFor: Table service and mixed fruit plates where looks matter.
products.skipIf: You want exact dimensions before buying.

products.name: Double-Sided Stainless Steel Grapefruit Knife with Hanging Loop
products.verdict: An all-metal single-piece knife with an angled tip and a hanging loop, for those who want storage flexibility.
products.description:
This is an all-stainless knife with serrated teeth on both blade edges, a narrow angled tip and a handle that includes a hanging loop. The tip is meant to run along the inner rind and between membranes, and the listing notes the working end has a distinct bend rather than one smooth curve.

It ranks last because it is the least refined in the group. An all-metal handle gets slippery with grapefruit juice, which is the one condition that matters here, and the listing offers few dimensions. The hanging loop is a real convenience if you keep tools on a rail, but it does not make up for a handle that has no grip texture.

Choose it if storage on a hook matters or you prefer a single-piece metal tool that will not crack. The caveat is that the manufacturer states it is for sectioning halved fruit only, so it is not a replacement for a paring knife.
products.idealFor: Kitchens that hang tools and want an unbreakable one-piece knife.
products.skipIf: You want a textured or cushioned grip.

methodology.title: Blade geometry
methodology.description: We compared curved, angled and straight serrated blades, since the shape decides whether a knife glides along a membrane or tears it.

methodology.title: Handle material and grip
methodology.description: Wood, nylon, oversized plastic and bare metal handles were scored for how well they hold when wet with juice.

methodology.title: Blade ends and reach
methodology.description: Listed blade lengths from 3.75 inches upward were checked against whether a second end handles the rind cut.

methodology.title: Care requirements
methodology.description: Dishwasher-safe and hand-wash-only instructions were weighed, since cleanup decides how often a small tool actually gets used.

methodology.title: Value within the bracket
methodology.description: Every knife here falls under $30, so feature depth was judged against that single price bucket.

whatMatters.detail: A grapefruit knife needs a curved edge that follows the membrane wall and fine serrations that saw through fibre without crushing it. Smooth blades slip and tear. On a listing, look for the words curved and serrated, and prefer teeth on both edges so you can work either side of a section.

Double-ended knives such as the Norpro Twin Blades and Fox Run 6601 carry one edge for the rind and another for the membrane, so you never swap tools. Single-ended knives like the Reluen and Chef Craft leave the rind cut to a paring knife. Check the product photo for a blade on each end.

Juice makes any handle slick within seconds. Rosewood and textured plastic hold better than bare metal, and a thicker diameter spreads pressure for tired hands. Look for words like non-slip or oversized, and be sceptical of an all-metal handle with no texture.

Listed overall lengths run from 7.5 to 8.75 inches here, and blade length matters more than total length. A 3.75 inch blade, as on the Chef Craft, reaches the center of a large half without your knuckles touching the rind. Look for a stated blade length.

Serrated grooves trap pulp, so a dishwasher-safe knife actually gets cleaned. Wood handles want a hand wash and a towel, while the Reluen and Norpro Nonstick list dishwasher cleaning. Check the care line on the listing, because wood and metal bonding can fail with repeated heat cycles.

howToChoose.intro: The number and shape of blade ends decides how much of the job one knife can do.

cards.label: Wood handle
cards.text: Wood gives heft and a controlled feel, and the Norpro Twin Blades, Chef Craft and Fox Run use it. It needs hand washing and a dry towel, and it can crack if left soaking.

cards.label: Plastic or nylon handle
cards.text: Molded handles shrug off water and heat. The Norpro Nonstick, Reluen and Better Houseware all tolerate the dishwasher, and the Norpro adds an oversized shape for larger hands.

howToChoose.note: Choose wood if you care about feel and will hand wash. Choose plastic or nylon if cleanup speed matters more.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A grip that does not fatigue across four or five fruit, a nonstick or smooth release so pulp does not clog the serrations, and dishwasher-safe cleanup after the guests leave.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Norpro Nonstick Squirtless suits a large batch because of its oversized handle and coating. The Reluen is the back-up if you also segment oranges for the same table.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You eat grapefruit daily and want a knife that feels balanced for years. The Norpro Twin Blades is the top step up in feel within this bracket.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You cut grapefruit occasionally. The Better Houseware nylon-handled knife does the same cut with less care and less fuss.

faq.q: Can I use a grapefruit knife on oranges and lemons?
faq.a: Yes. The Reluen is explicitly listed for oranges and lemons, and any curved, serrated blade such as the Chef Craft Select or Norpro Twin Blades will section them. Thin-skinned citrus is easier than grapefruit, so expect less effort.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake when sectioning grapefruit?
faq.a: Cutting the fruit in half through the stem axis instead of across the equator. Cutting across the segments exposes each wedge, which lets the Norpro Twin Blades or Fox Run 6601 follow the membrane lines properly.

faq.q: Is a double-ended knife worth it over a single blade?
faq.a: Yes if you do both cuts every time. The Norpro Twin Blades and Fox Run 6601 handle the rind and the membrane with one tool, while the Reluen and Chef Craft expect a separate paring knife.

faq.q: How do I hold the knife to avoid squirting juice?
faq.a: Cut the rind cut shallow and slide the blade along the membrane, rather than stabbing the center. Norpro markets its knives as squirt-reduced, but technique matters more, and a grip like the Norpro Nonstick helps control the angle.

faq.q: How should I clean a wood-handled grapefruit knife?
faq.a: Wash it by hand, rinse the serrations under running water and dry it right away. The Chef Craft Select specifically states hand wash only, and the Norpro Twin Blades rosewood handle behaves the same way.

faq.q: Do serrated grapefruit knives need sharpening?
faq.a: Serrated edges rarely need it, and home sharpening is hard because each tooth is a tiny curve. Replace a knife when the teeth stop catching fibre. On inexpensive pieces like the Better Houseware, replacement is the practical answer.

finalTake: Buy the Norpro Twin Blades if you want the classic knife done right, with two blade ends and a wooden grip that feels controlled. Choose the Norpro Nonstick Squirtless if an oversized handle and dishwasher cleanup matter more than the feel of wood. The Reluen is the right answer for households that segment all kinds of citrus and never want to hand wash. Every knife here costs under $30, so choose on handle and care, not price.
